en: [The Chapter on the Tree Flower] Dharma is the most excellent auspiciousness: non-violence, self-restraint, and austerity.
Even the gods pay homage to him whose mind is always fixed upon Dharma. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 1)

Just as a bee takes nectar from the flowers of a tree without harming the flower, and thereby nourishes itself; even so are these ascetics liberated who exist as virtuous ones in the world. (Dasaveyāliya 2)
Like birds among flowers, we should be intent on seeking alms;
thus we may obtain our livelihood and no one shall be harmed, moving among prepared foods like bees among flowers. (Dasavē. 3–4)
The Buddhas are like honey-gatherers; they are independent, restrained, and subsist on alms-food from various sources. Therefore, they are called "Sādhus. Thus I say. (Dasavēyāliya 5)
How indeed can one who does not restrain his desires, who falters at every step, and has fallen under the sway of his own thoughts, practice the life of a recluse? (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 6)
"He who does not enjoy clothes, perfumes, ornaments, women,
and beds out of lack of desire is not called a renunciant. (Dasavēyāliya 7) "And he who turns his back even on pleasant and dear enjoyments when they are obtained..."
He who abandons pleasures that are within his reach is indeed called a renouncer. (Dasavē.
8) While wandering with equanimity and right perception, if the mind should stray outward, he should train himself thus:
"She is not mine, nor am I hers. In this way, he should subdue passion. (Dasavē. 9)
Enter the fire, cast off the garland of grief, and enjoy sensual pleasures; for suffering is indeed conquered by those who have enjoyed them.
Cut off hatred and subdue passion; thus you will become happy in the life hereafter. (Dasaveyāliya 10) One might leap into a blazing fire, smoking and difficult to approach.
"Those born in noble families do not wish to eat what has been vomited. Fie on you, seeker of fame and glory!
You who desire to swallow again that which you have vomited for the sake of life—death would be better for you. (Dasaveyāliya 11–12)
I am [the son] of Bhogarāja, and you are the blind cowherd;
let us not be a disgrace to our family. Practice self-restraint with a tranquil mind. (Dasavē.
13) If you harbor such an intention toward whatever women you see—
"You will become one whose soul is tormented by remorse, like a fish struck by a hook. (Dasavē.
14) Having heard those well-spoken words of Sañjayā, he turned toward the Dharma, just as an elephant is restrained by a goad. (Dasavē. 15)
Thus do the perfectly awakened ones, the wise and discerning, turn away from enjoyments, just like that supreme man. Thus I say. (Dasavē. 16)
[The Story of Minor Conduct] For those protectors who are well-established in self-restraint and completely liberated—
These are the things not permitted for those naked ascetics, the great sages:
food set aside for them, food purchased, food brought from elsewhere, eating at night, bathing, perfumes and garlands, and fans. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 17–18)
Storing [food], [accepting] what is intended for a householder, royal alms, and food obtained by begging;
massaging, cleaning the teeth, inquiring after one's health, and looking at one's own body; and sitting on a raised seat, using a measuring vessel, and carrying an umbrella. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 19)
The mendicant should avoid medical treatment,
footwear for the feet, and the kindling of fire; (he should also avoid) food provided by the bed-maker, chairs,
couches, sitting on the threshold between houses, and the rubbing of the body.
Service rendered for householders, that which pertains to the livelihood of others, eating from a heated vessel, and seeking refuge when ill;
radish, ginger, sugarcane, and unboiled sugar-cane juice. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 22)
[One should not consume] bulbs, roots, or anything containing living beings, nor raw fruits or seeds. (Dasavē.
23) Sovaccala salt, Sindhava salt, Romālava salt, sea salt, Paṃsukhāra salt, and Kālālōṇa salt—these too, when raw, [are forbidden]. (Dasavē. 24)
Fumigation, emetics, enemas, purgatives, collyrium, tooth-cleaning, and the anointing and ornamentation of the body— these ten (Dasavē.
25) are all unallowable for the great seers who are Nirgranthas.

For those who are engaged in self-restraint and who move with lightness— Having fully understood the five influxes, guarded in three ways, restrained in six, and having conquered the five [senses], the wise Nigganthas are straight-visioned. (Dasavē. 26–27)
In the summer they expose themselves to the heat; in the winter they remain uncovered; in the rains they stay secluded—thus the self-restrained ones are well-composed.
With their enemies in the form of the afflictions subdued, with delusion shaken off, and with their senses conquered.
The great seers, having abandoned all suffering, depart;
having exhausted their former karmas through self-restraint and austerity, those protectors have attained the path of perfection and are fully extinguished. (Dasavēyāliya 29–30)
Thus I say.
[The Six Classes of Living Beings]

I have heard, O venerable one, that this chapter named *Ṣaḍjīvanikā* was indeed proclaimed here by the Blessed One, the ascetic Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa; it has been well-expounded and well-proclaimed. It is good for me to study this chapter, this exposition of the Dharma. What indeed is that chapter named *Ṣaḍjīvanikā*, proclaimed by the ascetic Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa, which has been well-expounded and well-proclaimed, and which is good for me to study as an exposition of the Dharma?

This indeed is the chapter named *Ṣaḍjīvaṇīya* (The Six Classes of Living Beings), proclaimed by the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra, the Kāśyapa; it is well-expounded and well-proclaimed. It is beneficial for me to study this chapter, the exposition of Dharma, which is as follows: 1. Earth-bodied beings (*puḍhavikāiya*). 2. Water-bodied beings (*āukāiya*). 3. Fire-bodied beings (*tēukāiya*). 4. Air-bodied beings (*vāukāiya*). 5. Plant-bodied beings (*vaṇassaïkāiya*). 6. Mobile-bodied beings (*tasakāiya*). Earth is declared to possess consciousness (*cittamanta*); it consists of many souls (*anēgajīvā*) existing separately (*puḍhōsattā*), except where there is transformation by means of weapons (*satthapariṇaēṇaṁ*). Water is declared to possess consciousness; it consists of many souls existing separately, except where there is transformation by means of weapons. Fire is declared to possess consciousness; it consists of many souls existing separately, except where there is transformation by means of weapons. Air is declared to possess consciousness; it consists of many souls existing separately, except where there is transformation by means of weapons. Plants are declared to possess consciousness; they consist of many souls existing separately, except where there is transformation by means of weapons. They are as follows: those propagated from seeds at the tip (*aggabīya*), those propagated from roots (*mūlabīya*), those propagated from joints (*porabīya*), those propagated from stems (*khandhabīya*), those that grow from seeds (*bīyarūha*), and those that arise spontaneously (*samucchima*). Grasses, creepers, and plant-bodied beings that possess seeds are declared to possess consciousness; they consist of many souls existing separately, except where there is transformation by means of weapons.

Furthermore, those many and numerous mobile beings (*trasa-prāṇas*) are as follows: those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, those born from fluids, those born from germination, those born by spontaneous generation, those born from sprouts, and those born from transformation; those of whatever living beings there may be who move forward and backward, contract and expand, who crawl, wander, tremble, flee, and who are known by their coming and going; and those which are insects and beetles, and those which are ants and termites—all two-sensed beings, all three-sensed beings, all four-sensed beings, all five-sensed beings, all animal-born beings, all hell-beings, all human beings, all gods, and all living beings belonging to the supreme order of existence—this indeed is called the sixth category of living beings, the category of mobile beings (*trasa-kāya*).

Thus, regarding these six classes of living beings, one should not oneself inflict violence, nor cause others to inflict violence, nor approve of others inflicting violence; for as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. For that, O Venerable One, I confess, I blame, I censure, and I renounce myself.

O Venerable One, in the first great vow, there is abstention from the destruction of living beings. O Venerable One, I renounce all destruction of living beings—whether subtle or gross, mobile or immobile. Neither shall I myself destroy living beings, nor shall I cause others to destroy living beings, nor do I approve of others destroying living beings. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not commit [this act], I do not cause it to be committed, and I do not approve of another who commits it. O Venerable One, I turn back from that; I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish my own self. O Venerable One, I am established in the first great vow: abstention from all destruction of living beings.

Furthermore, O Venerable One, there is the second great vow: abstention from false speech. O Venerable One, I renounce all false speech—whether out of anger, greed, fear, or amusement. I myself shall not speak falsely, nor shall I cause others to speak falsely, nor shall I approve of others who speak falsely. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I shall neither do it, nor cause it to be done, nor approve of it being done by another. O Venerable One, I turn away from that; I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish myself [from such conduct]. O Venerable One, I am established in the second great vow: abstention from all false speech.

Furthermore, venerable sir, there is this third great vow: abstention from taking what is not given. Venerable sir, I renounce all taking of what is not given—whether in a village, a city, or a forest; whether little or much, fine or coarse, animate or inanimate. Neither shall I myself take what is not given, nor shall I cause others to take what is not given, nor shall I approve of others who take what is not given. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. Venerable sir, I turn back from that; I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish myself [from such conduct]. Venerable sir, I am established in this third great vow: abstention from all taking of what is not given.

Furthermore, O Venerable One, there is the fourth great vow: abstention from sexual intercourse. O Venerable One, I renounce all sexual intercourse—whether divine, human, or pertaining to the animal realm. Neither shall I myself engage in sexual intercourse, nor shall I cause others to engage in sexual intercourse, nor shall I approve of others who are engaging in sexual intercourse. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not perform it, I do not cause it to be performed, and I do not approve of another who performs it. For that, O Venerable One, I confess, I blame, I censure, and I relinquish myself. O Venerable One, I am established in the fourth great vow: abstention from all sexual intercourse.

Furthermore, venerable sir, there is the fifth great vow: abstention from possession (*parigraha*). Venerable sir, I renounce all possession—whether it be little or much, minute or large, animate or inanimate. I myself shall not take possession, nor shall I cause others to take possession, nor shall I approve of others taking possession. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not act, I do not cause to be done, and I do not approve of another who is acting. Venerable sir, I turn back from that; I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish my own self. Venerable sir, I am established in the fifth great vow: abstention from all possession.

Furthermore, O Venerable One, there is the sixth vow: abstention from eating at night. O Venerable One, I renounce all eating at night—whether it be food, drink, soft food, or delicacies. Neither shall I eat at night myself, nor cause others to eat at night, nor do I approve of others eating at night. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. For that, O Venerable One, I confess, I blame, I censure, and I relinquish myself. O Venerable One, I am established in the sixth vow: abstention from all eating at night.
Thus, having undertaken these five great vows, with the abstention from eating at night as the sixth, for the sake of my own welfare, I dwell [in them].

Whether it be a monk or a nun, who has restrained themselves, desisted from evil, and renounced sinful actions—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, asleep or awake—that person, with respect to earth, clay, stone, or a clod of earth, or with respect to a body covered in dust or a garment covered in dust, shall not scratch, nor scrape, nor strike, nor break it with their hand, foot, wood, broom, finger, or a stone-tool, nor with a tool held in the hand; they shall not cause another to scratch, scrape, strike, or break it; nor shall they approve of another scratching, scraping, striking, or breaking it. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. O Venerable One, I turn away from that, I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish myself.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, who is self-restrained, disciplined, and has turned back from and renounced evil karma—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, whether asleep or awake—that person, [regarding] water, dew, frost, mist, hoarfrost, young grass, or pure water; or a body moist with water, or a garment moist with water; or a body that is damp, or a garment that is damp—should not touch it, should not come into contact with it, should not rub it, should not scrub it, should not shake it, should not shake it about; should not warm it, should not cause it to be warmed; nor should they cause another to touch it, cause another to come into contact with it, cause another to rub it, cause another to scrub it, cause another to shake it, cause another to shake it about, cause another to warm it, or cause another to cause it to be warmed; nor should they approve of another touching it, coming into contact with it, rubbing it, scrubbing it, shaking it, shaking it about, warming it, or causing it to be warmed. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. O Venerable One! I repent of that, I blame it, I censure it, and I relinquish myself.

Whether he be a monk or a nun, who has restrained himself, who is free from passion, and who has warded off and renounced evil karma—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, asleep or awake—he shall not touch fire, nor embers, nor glowing coals, nor flames, nor sparks, nor a firebrand, nor a pure flame, nor hot water; he shall not stir it, nor strike it, nor break it, nor kindle it, nor cause it to blaze up, nor extinguish it. He shall not cause another to touch it, nor to strike it, nor to break it, nor to kindle it, nor to cause it to blaze up, nor to extinguish it. Nor shall he approve of another who touches it, strikes it, breaks it, kindles it, causes it to blaze up, or extinguishes it. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. O Venerable One, I turn away from that; I blame it, I censure it, and I renounce myself.

Whether he be a monk or a nun, one who has restrained himself, desisted from evil, and renounced sinful karma—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, asleep or awake—he shall not blow upon, nor fan with his own body, another person, or anything external, using a fan, a whisk, a palm-leaf fan, a leaf, a leaf-fragment, a branch, a twig, a peacock-feather fan, a hand-fan, a cloth, a corner of a garment, or even with his own hand or mouth. He shall not cause another to blow or fan, nor shall he approve of another blowing or fanning. For as long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. O Venerable One! I repent of that; I blame it, I condemn it, and I renounce myself.

Whether he be a monk or a nun, who has restrained himself, who is free from passion, and who has desisted from and renounced evil karma—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, asleep or awake—he shall not walk upon seeds, nor upon those containing seeds, nor upon sprouts, nor upon those containing sprouts, nor upon plants, nor upon those containing plants, nor upon greenery, nor upon those containing greenery, nor upon what is cut, nor upon what contains what is cut, nor upon anything with life, nor upon anything resting on that which has life. He shall not walk there, nor stand, nor sit, nor lie down; he shall not cause another to walk, stand, sit, or lie down; nor shall he approve of another walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. As long as life lasts, in three ways and by three means—through mind, speech, and body—I do not do it, I do not cause it to be done, and I do not approve of another doing it. O Venerable One! I repent of that, I blame it, I censure it, and I renounce myself.

Whether it be a monk or a nun, who has restrained themselves, desisted from evil, and renounced sinful karma—whether by day or by night, alone or in a group, asleep or awake—if they see an insect, a moth, an ant, or a termite upon their hand, foot, arm, thigh, belly, head, or upon their robe, alms-bowl, blanket, broom, dust-remover, whisk, staff, stool, plank, bed, or bedding, or upon any other such kind of equipment, they should, being self-restrained, repeatedly inspect and repeatedly wipe it, and then set it aside in a secluded spot; they must not cause injury to living beings.
Moving about without self-control, one harms living beings and binds sinful karma; that results in bitter fruit for him.
Standing without self-control, one likewise harms living beings. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 4.7)
One who acts without self-restraint binds sinful karma; that results in bitter fruit for him. (Dasavē.
48) Furthermore, one who moves about without self-restraint harms living beings and binds sinful karma; that results in bitter fruit for him. (Dasavē. 49)
One who lies down without self-restraint harms living beings and binds sinful karma;
that results in bitter fruit for him. One who eats without self-restraint harms living beings. (Dasavaikālika Sūtra 5.50)
One who speaks without restraint binds sinful karma; that results in bitter fruit for him. (Dasavē.
51) Indeed, one who speaks without restraint harms living beings;
he binds sinful karma, and that results in bitter fruit for him. (Dasavē. 52)
How should one walk? How should one stand? How should one sit? How should one lie down?
How should one eat? How should one speak so that one does not bind evil karma?
One should walk with restraint, stand with restraint, sit with restraint, and lie down with restraint. (Dasaveyāliya 5.3)
While enjoying victory, speaking, or performing purifying deeds, one does not bind evil karma. (Dasavē.
54) For one who regards all beings as himself, who perceives beings correctly, whose influxes are closed, and who is self-controlled, evil karma is not bound. (Dasavē. 55)
First comes knowledge, and from that, compassion; thus it stands for all the self-restrained.
What will the ignorant one do, or how shall he know the distinction between merit and evil?
Having heard, one knows what is auspicious; having heard, one knows what is evil.
Having understood both, one should practice that which is beneficial. (Dasavē.
57) He who does not know living beings, nor does he know non-living beings;
how can he, not knowing both living and non-living beings, know self-restraint? (Dasavē. 58)
He who understands the living being and also understands the non-living being—
knowing both the living and the non-living— he indeed knows self-restraint. (Dasaveyāliya 5.9) When he understands both these two, the living and the non-living...
By that [knowledge], he knows the various destinies of all living beings. (Dasavē.
60) When he knows the various destinies of all living beings, then he knows merit and demerit, as well as bondage and liberation. (Dasavē. 61)
When one knows both merit and evil, as well as bondage and liberation, then one should become indifferent to enjoyments, whether they be divine or human. (Dasavē.
62) When one becomes indifferent to enjoyments, whether they be divine or human...
By that [means], one abandons attachment, both internal and external. (Dasavē.
63) When one abandons attachment, both internal and external, then, having become shaven-headed, one goes forth into the homeless state. (Dasavē. 64)
When, having become shaven-headed and having gone forth into the homeless state, one then touches the unsurpassed Dharma of supreme restraint. (Dasavē.
65) When one touches the unsurpassed Dharma of supreme restraint...
By that [practice], one shakes off the dust of karma and the impurity accumulated through ignorance. (Dasavē.
66) When one shakes off the dust of karma and the impurity accumulated through ignorance, then one attains all-pervading knowledge and insight. (Dasavē. 67)
When he attains all-encompassing knowledge and vision, then the Jina,
as a Kevalin, knows both the world and the non-world. (Dasaveyāliya 6.8) When the Jina, as a Kevalin, knows both the world and the non-world...
Having restrained the activities by means of that [meditation], he attains the state of the mountain-peak (śaileśī).

When, having restrained the activities, he attains the state of the mountain-peak, then, having exhausted his karma, he becomes free from passion and goes to perfection (siddhi). (Daśavaikālika 6.69–70)
When, having exhausted karma, he attains perfection free from passion, then, established at the summit of the world, he becomes an eternal Siddha. (Dasavē.
71) For a monk who relishes pleasure, who is agitated by sensual desires, and who is a consumer of worldly goods—

For one who destroys his own progress by indulging in luxuries, a good rebirth is difficult to attain. (Dasavēyāliya 72) But for one who is preeminent in the virtues of austerity, whose mind is upright, who is devoted to patience and self-restraint, and who conquers the hardships, a good rebirth is easily attained. (Dasavēyāliya 73)

Even later, those offspring quickly go to the abodes of the immortals for whom there is love for austerity, self-restraint, patience, and celibacy. Thus, one with right view should always strive in this sixfold code of conduct. (Dasaveyāliya 7.4)
Having obtained the ascetic life, which is difficult to attain, you should not bring it to ruin through your actions. Thus I say. (Dasavēyāliya 7.5)
When the time for alms has arrived, one should seek food and drink with this method of action—unperturbed and unattached. (Dasavē. 7.6)
Whether in a village or a town, the sage should wander slowly and without agitation for alms, with an undistracted mind.
Looking ahead only the distance of a yoke, he should walk while scanning the ground.
One should avoid seeds and green plants, living beings, water, and clay.
(Dasavē. 78) One should avoid a slope, uneven ground, a stump, and a marshy place;
one should not cross by a precarious path when a safe way exists. (Dasavē. 79)
While falling or stumbling there, the restrained one might harm living beings, whether mobile or stationary. Therefore, the restrained one, well-composed, should not go there. (Dasavē. 8.80)
He should go by another path; he should exert himself only in what is right. (Dasavē.
81) O Gautama, being self-restrained, one should not step over a heap of embers, a heap of ashes, or a heap of chaff with feet that have dust upon them. (Dasavē. 82)
One should not wander during the rains when it is raining, nor when the earth is falling apart, nor when a great wind is blowing, nor where there are creatures moving crosswise. (Dasavē.
83) One should not wander in the vicinity of women, for one who is devoted to celibacy [must avoid such places].
For one who practices self-restraint and is self-controlled, there may arise therein a loss of faith.

For one wandering in what is not a proper resort, through constant association [with the unwholesome], there may be an affliction of the vows and doubt regarding the state of asceticism. (Dasavē. 84–85)
Therefore, having understood this, the sage, dwelling in solitude, should avoid the fault that increases one's miserable rebirths— the presence of a border-guard.
[One should avoid] a bitch with puppies, a cow about to give birth, a fierce bull, a horse, or an elephant.

One should avoid from afar quarreling, strife, and combat. (Dasavēyāliya 8.7) Neither haughty nor humble, not elated and undisturbed, having subdued the senses according to their respective domains, the sage should wander. (Dasavēyāliya 8.8)

One should not go hurrying; while speaking during one's alms-round, one should not approach with laughter. One should always avoid high and low families [for alms], as well as houses with open windows, lattices, doors, and those with concealed openings. (Dasavēyāliya 8.9)

While wandering, one should not look with lustful intent; one should avoid places of danger. (Dasaveyāliya 9.90) One should avoid from afar those places that cause defilement, such as those belonging to kings, householders, and secret guards. (Dasaveyāliya 9.91)
One should not enter a censured family; one should avoid a family that is indifferent; one should not enter a family that is hostile, but should enter a family that is hospitable. (Dasavē.
92) One should not oneself pull open a door closed by a curtain or a screen.

One who has not received formal permission should not push open a door-panel. Having entered the alms-round, one should not delay with excrement or urine; having recognized a suitable space and having requested permission, one should discharge them. (Dasavēyāliya 93–94)
One should avoid a dark doorway or a storehouse where there are eye-poisonous creatures that are difficult to inspect. (Dasavē.
95) Where flowers and seeds are scattered about in a storehouse...

Having seen a house recently smeared with plaster, one should avoid it [by not crossing over]. (Dasaveyāliya 9.6) A self-controlled monk should not enter a stable after having stepped over a young elephant, a child, a dog, or even a calf, nor should he enter by pushing them aside. (Dasaveyāliya 9.7)
He should look without becoming attached; he should not gaze from too close a distance, nor should he stare with wide-open eyes.
Restraining himself, he should not speak excessively. A sage who has gone out for alms should not go beyond the proper limit. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 9.8)
Having understood the ground of the household, one should exert oneself with moderation on that ground. (Dasavē.
99) Therein, being skilled in the examination of the ground, one should inspect the place for bathing and the latrine, and avoid any accumulation [of waste]. (Dasavē. 100)
Avoiding water with soil, seeds, and green plants, he should remain standing, composed in all his senses.
While he is standing there, his food and drink consist of solid and liquid nourishment.
One should not accept what is improper; one should accept what is proper. (Dasavē.
102) If, while eating there, one should cause the food to be scattered, one should refuse the giver, saying: "Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē. 103)
Trampling upon living beings, seeds, and green plants, one should avoid such an act, knowing it to be an act of non-restraint. (Dasavē.
104) Having gathered [things] and having set them down, and having touched that which possesses life.
Likewise, for the sake of a śramaṇa, having stirred up water;
having plunged into it or moved about in it, one who gives food and drink—one should refuse such [food], saying: "It is not allowable for me. (Dasavē. 105–106)
If someone is giving with a hand that has been previously prepared, or with a ladle, or with a vessel, he should refuse it, saying:
"Such a thing is not permissible for me. Likewise [if the food is] wet, moist, dusty, or mixed with clay. (Dasavē.
Haritāla, hiṅgulaka, manaḥśilā, añjana, and lavaṇa—these are the ten [minerals]. (Dasav.
108) Gairika, varṇika, seḍīya, soraṭṭhiya, piṭṭha, kukkusa, kāya, ukkiṭṭha, asaṃsaṭṭha, and saṃsaṭṭha are also to be understood. (Dasav. 109)
One should not desire food being given with a hand that is not clean, or with a ladle or a vessel,
where subsequent processing (pacchākamma) would take place.
[Dasavēyāliya Sutta 110] With a hand that is clean, or with a ladle or a vessel...

One should accept what is being given that is suitable for seeking (eṣaṇīya). (Dasavē. 111) But when two people are eating, if one among them invites [the monk], he should not desire what is being given; he should examine the donor's intention. (Dasavē. 112)
When two people are eating together, one may accept the food being offered if both are invited there; it should be that which is suitable for seeking (eṣaṇīya).
[Daśavaikālika 11.3] Regarding a pregnant woman, various kinds of drinks and foods may be presented.
One should avoid [food] while she is eating; one should accept the remainder of her meal. (Dasavē.
114) Furthermore, for the sake of a monk, a pregnant woman who is near her time, or one who has stood up, might sit down;
or one who is seated might stand up again. (Dasavē. 115)
That food and drink, however, is not permissible for the Sañjayas; one should refuse it when being offered, saying, "Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē.
11.6) [This applies even if] a breast is being sucked by a child or a young girl.
Having set aside that food, drink, and meal while weeping—Dasavē.
117—that food and drink would be improper for the self-controlled (sañjaya); one should refuse it, saying, "Such a thing is not allowable for me. Dasavē. 118.
Whatever food or drink there may be that is suspected as being either allowable or unallowable, one should decline it when it is being offered, saying: "Such a thing is not allowable for me. [Dasavē.
119] If it is covered by a water-strainer, a cloth, or a stand...

Whether with a paste made from flour, or with some kind of resin—if one should break open [the vessel] and give it, or cause it to be given for the sake of a recluse, he should refuse the giver, saying: "Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē. 120–121)
Whether it be food, drink, or likewise hard food and soft food—
whatever one should know of or hear regarding this, that it has been prepared for the purpose of giving— that food and drink is not permissible for the self-restrained. (Dasavēyāliya 12.2)

One should renounce such food; it is not permissible for me [to consume] such food, drink, soft food, or hard food, whether one knows of it or hears of it, that it has been prepared for the sake of merit. (Daśavaikālika 12.3–4)
If someone offers food or drink that is improper for the Sañjayas, one should refuse it, saying: "Such a thing is not permissible for me. (Dasavē.
125) This applies to solid food, drink, as well as soft food and refreshments.

Whatever one might know or hear regarding this manifest form of trade, that food and drink is not permissible for the self-restrained; one should refuse it from the giver, saying, "Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē. 126–127)
Whether it be a seat, a drink, or likewise solid or soft food—
whatever one should know or hear to have been prepared for the sake of a śramaṇa— that food and drink is not permissible for the self-restrained. (Dasavēyāliya 12.8)
One should reject what is given for a second time; such things are not permissible for me. (Dasavē.

129) One should avoid food that is specially prepared for a monk, food purchased, food offered as a sacrifice, food brought from elsewhere, food stored overnight, food received on credit, and food mixed with other types of impure alms. (Dasavē. 130)
Furthermore, one should inquire about its origin: for whom was it intended, and by whom was it made?
Having heard that it is pure and free from doubt, the self-restrained monk should accept it.
This applies to food, drink, or likewise, solid and soft edibles. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 5.1.31)

If there should be a mixture among the flowers, or among the seeds, or among the green vegetables—such food and drink is not allowable for the self-restrained; one should refuse it, saying, "Such a thing is not permissible for me. (Dasavē. 132–133)

Whether it be a seat, a drink, or likewise solid food or soft food, if it has been placed in water or among insects and fungi, that food and drink is not permissible for the self-restrained. (Dasavē. 134)

One should renounce such things; it is not permissible for me [to accept] food, drink, or likewise solid or soft food that has been placed in fire, or which one gives after having touched it. (Daśavaikālika 135–136)
That food and drink, O Sañjayas, which is not permissible for those who have renounced the world, one should refuse when it is being offered, saying: "Such a thing is not permissible for me. (Dasavē.
137) Likewise, [one should refuse] that which has been heated and then cooled, or that which has been extinguished after being kindled.

Having poured out, having poured down, having turned over, or having covered it—such food and drink, O restrained ones, is not allowable for those who are self-controlled; one should refuse it, saying, "Such as this is not allowable for me. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 138–139)

Whether it be wood, stone, or even brick, if at some time it has been placed for the purpose of a bridge, and that [bridge] should be movable or unstable—a monk should not go upon it; for if seen there, there is lack of self-restraint. (Dasavēyāliya 140)
Deep and indeed hollow, with all his senses concentrated— having climbed up by means of a ladder, a plank,
a stool, a couch, a pillar, or a palace, he should provide such things for the sake of the ascetic. (Dasaveyāliya 141–142)
While climbing up, one might fall, or might injure a hand or a foot;
one might harm earth-beings and those creatures in the world that depend upon them. Having recognized such great faults, the great sages [avoid them]. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 5.1.43)

Therefore, the self-controlled do not accept alms that have been brought for them on a string. (Dasaveyāliya 144) One should avoid raw bulbs, roots, or hanging fruits; likewise, one should avoid raw, cut, or unripened gourds, as well as raw *tumbāga* and *siṅgabēra*. (Dasaveyāliya 145)
Likewise, rice flour, jujube flour, cakes, molasses, sweetmeats, or any other such food being sold openly in the market, having been touched with passion [by the seller]. (Dasavē.
One should refuse what is given; such things are not permissible for me:
a person with many bones, or one with unblinking eyes, or one with many thorns;
a thorn-apple, a *tinduka* fruit, a *bilva* fruit, a piece of sugarcane, or a *śimbali* flower. (Daśavaikālika 147–148)

If there should be food of his own that has been largely discarded, he should not refuse it when a righteous person offers it, thinking, "Such a thing is not permissible for me. Likewise, [he should not refuse] various kinds of drinks, or even water used for rinsing.
One should avoid rice-water that has been recently washed. (Dasavē.

150) But that which one knows to have been washed long ago, either by means of intelligence or by observation, or having inquired about it or heard of it, and which has become free from doubt—(Dasavē. 151)
Having understood that it is inanimate matter, the restrained one may accept it; however, if it should be suspected [of being animate], one should not eat it after having tasted it. (Dasavē.
152) "Give me a small amount in your hand for the purpose of tasting. (Dasavē. 153)
"Let me not have this very sour food; it is not fit to be eaten. (Dasavē.
153) If someone gives him that very sour food, [thinking] "it is not fit to be eaten," he should refuse it, saying:
"Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē. 154)

And if that [food] has been accepted unwillingly or with a dejected mind, he should not drink it himself, nor should he give it to another. Having gone to a secluded place and inspected it carefully, [he should dispose of it]. (Dasavē. 155)
One should announce the victory [of finding food]; having announced it, one should depart. (Dasavē.
156) If, while returning from the alms-round, one should desire to eat at a stable, or at the base of a wall, one should inspect it and [ensure it is] pure. (Dasavē. 157)
Having obtained permission, the wise one, being restrained and composed, should thoroughly wipe his hand and eat there with self-control.
While he is eating there, there might be a bone or a thorn [in his food]. (Daśavaikālika 158)
Whether it be grass, wood, or gravel, or any other such thing, having picked it up, one should not throw it away;
one should not discard it with expectation, nor should one pick it up with the hand and then cast it aside. Having taken it, one should go to a secluded spot. (Dasavē. 159–160)
Having gone to a secluded place and having discarded what has been accumulated, one should dispose of the alms; having disposed of them, one should perform the *pratikramaṇa*. (Dasavē.
161) It may be that a monk, having approached his dwelling, should wish to eat.

Having approached with alms-food and having discarded the water-pot, the sage, having entered with discipline into the presence of the teacher, and having performed the *iriyāvahiya* [expiation], should confess his arrival. (Dasavē. 162–163)
Having fully confessed every transgression in due order regarding going and coming,
as well as food and drink, the self-restrained one, straightforward in thought, undisturbed, and with an unperturbed mind— (Dasavēyāliya 164).

One should confess before the Guru whatever has been undertaken as it was. (Daśavaikālika 165) If one has not properly confessed what was done previously or afterwards, one should again perform repentance for that; having renounced [worldly attachments], one should reflect thus: (Daśavaikālika 166)
"Aho! The Jinas have taught a blameless livelihood for the ascetics;
it is excellent that they maintain their bodies for the sake of achieving liberation. (Dasaveyāliya 167) Having recited the *namokkāra* and performed the praise of the Jina...
Having undertaken the recitation of the scriptures, the sage should rest for a moment.
While resting, he should reflect upon this beneficial purpose: "If the Blessed One would show me favor, it would be well; I would be one who has been delivered. (Dasavē. 168–169)
One should invite one's companions with respect according to their seniority;
if some among them should desire it, one should eat together with them. But if no one should desire it, then one may eat alone. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 170)
A wise person should examine the vessel; [he should eat] with self-restraint, without spilling. (Dasavē.

171) Whether it be bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, sweet, or salty—having obtained such food prepared for another purpose, the self-controlled one should consume it like honey or ghee. (Dasavē. 172)
Whether it be tasteless or flavorless, seasoned or unseasoned, wet or even dry—
whether it be a meal of parched grain or groats— one should not despise what has been obtained, provided it is pure, whether in small or large quantity. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 173)
One who obtains food easily and lives by righteous means should eat while avoiding faults.
(Dasavēyāliya 174) Those who give gifts easily are rare, and those who live by righteous means are also rare.
Both the one who gives easily and the one who lives by righteous means go to a happy destination. (Dasavēyāliya 175)

Thus I say: Having wiped the alms-bowl with care, the self-restrained one should consume whatever is there, whether it be foul-smelling or fragrant; he should not discard anything. (Dasavaikālika 176)
Having eaten for the sake of austerity while staying in his lodging or on his alms-round,
if he cannot sustain himself with that [food],
then when a specific reason has arisen, he should seek food and drink. (Daśavaikālika 5.1.77)

By the former rule and by this latter one, a monk should go forth at the proper time and return at the proper time; avoiding the improper time, he should practice at the proper time. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 178–179)
"You wander for alms at the wrong time, O monk; you do not observe the proper time, you weary yourself, and you revile the settlement.
"At the right time should the monk wander; he should perform his manly duty. (Dasavē. 180)
One should not be distressed by lack of gain; rather, one should endure it as penance. (Dasavē.
181) Likewise, when various living beings have gathered for the sake of food, one should not go straight toward them, but should proceed with careful restraint. (Dasavē. 182)
Having entered for alms, one should not sit down anywhere, nor should one engage in conversation; remaining restrained, one should stand still.
A restrained monk should avoid a bolt, a threshold, a door, or even a door-panel.
A sage who has gone forth on his alms-round should not stand waiting.
Whether it be a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a pauper, or a traveler, the self-restrained one should approach them for the sake of food or drink. (Dasavēyāliya 184–185)

One should not enter after having transgressed that [boundary], nor should one stand within the range of vision [of those inside]. Having retreated to a secluded spot, the self-restrained one should stand there.
This applies to the mendicant, or to the donor, or to both. (Dasaveyāliya 186)
There may be a lack of faith, or there may be a lightening of the teaching.
Whether [food] has been refused or given, once that [person] has turned back, the restrained one may approach for the sake of food or for the sake of drink. (Dasavē. 187–188)

Whether it be a blue lotus, a red lotus, a night-lotus, or a *magadantī*, or any other flower that possesses life—having plucked such a thing, one should not give it as food or drink; for that is improper for the self-restrained (*sañjaya*). (Dasavē. 189)
One should renounce [the use of] flowers; such a thing is not permissible for me.
Whether it be a blue lotus, a red lotus, a night-blooming water lily, a jasmine, or any other flower that is still living, one should not give it after having crushed it. (Dasavē. 190–191)
If someone offers that food or drink which is unallowable for the Sañjayas, he should refuse it, saying: "Such a thing is not allowable for me. (Dasavē.
192) Whether it be water-lily root, lotus stalk, lily, or blue-lily stalk—
The lotus stalk, the sprout of the *sāsava* plant, and the unboiled sugarcane rind;
tender sprouts of a tree, of grass, or of any other green herb—one should avoid these while they are raw. (Dasavē. 193–194)
If a young woman is offering a chickpea cake (*chivāḍī*) that has been moistened and fried, he should refuse it, saying:
"Such a thing is not allowable for me.
Likewise, [he should refuse] *kōla* soaked in water, bamboo shoots, or *kāsavanālika*.
One should avoid raw sesame cakes;
likewise, one should avoid raw rice flour, or rice-water that has not been cooled by heat, as well as sesame meal, *pūi*, and raw *pinnāga*. (Dasavēyāliya 196–197)
One should not even mentally desire jackfruit, mangoes, radishes, or *mūlagattiya*—if they are raw and not yet transformed by fire.
Likewise, one should recognize the flour of fruits and the flour of seeds [as unfit for consumption]. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 19.8)
One should avoid the *bihēlaga* and the *piyāla* fruits while they are unripe. (Dasavē.
199) A monk should always wander for alms from high and low families;
having passed through humble families, he should not dwell upon those that are prosperous. (Dasavē. 200)
One should seek one's livelihood without being dejected; the wise person should not despair.
Being moderate in eating, one should be intent on the rules of proper alms-gathering (*eṣaṇā*).
There is much in the houses of others—various kinds of food and snacks. (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 2.1b)
A wise person should not become angry in that situation, whether another gives what is desired or not. (Dasavē.
202) Whether it be bedding, a seat, clothing, food, or drink, a self-controlled one should not be angry with one who does not give; rather, one should simply renounce it. (Dasavē. 203)
Whether it be a woman or a man, whether young or old, one should not show anger toward one who salutes, nor should one speak harshly to them.
He who is not saluted should not be provoked to anger, and he who has been saluted should not exalt himself. (Dasaveyāliya 204)
Thus, while living as one who has attained [the goal], he practices the life of a renunciant. (Dasavē.
205) It may happen that a certain person, having obtained [food], conceals it out of greed, thinking:
"Let this not be given away," and seeing it, consumes it himself. (Dasavē. 206)
One who is greedy for his own sake, a wicked person, commits much evil and becomes difficult to satisfy; he does not attain nirvāṇa. (Dasavē.
207) Suppose one person were to obtain various kinds of food and drink.
Having eaten what is excellent, one should take that which is discolored and tasteless.
Let these ascetics know: this sage, seeking his own welfare, contented, resorts to solitude; he is of simple livelihood and easily satisfied. (Dasavē. 208–209)
One who seeks honor for the sake of worship, or who desires respect and praise, produces much evil and creates the dart of deceit. (Dasavē.
210) Whether it be liquor, wine, or any other intoxicating substance—
A monk should not drink [liquor] while it is being watched; he should guard his own reputation. (Dasavē.
211) One may be a thief who loves solitude, thinking, "No one knows me.
Behold his faults, and hear from me of his deceit. (Dasavē. 212)
The intoxication of that monk increases, along with deceit, falsehood, infamy, and the lack of liberation;
he is constantly regarded as unvirtuous.
Like a thief who is perpetually anxious due to his own deeds, so is the one of evil intent. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 213)
Such a person, even at the time of death, does not achieve self-restraint. Such a person does not honor the teacher, nor do they honor the ascetic;
even householders reproach such a person because they recognize him for what he is. (Dasavē. 214–215)
But one who thus seeks out faults and avoids virtues—even at the time of death—does not achieve self-restraint. (Dasavē.
216) The wise man practices austerity and avoids exquisite flavors.
The ascetic who has abandoned intoxication and negligence is one of supreme excellence.
Behold his auspiciousness, which is honored by many holy men; it is vast and endowed with great purpose. I shall proclaim it; listen to me. (Dasaveyāliya 217–218)
Thus, one who perceives virtues and avoids vices, even at the end of life, maintains self-restraint;
such a person honors both the teacher and the ascetic. (Dasavē. 219)
Even householders are not honored if they recognize such a person:
a man who is a thief of austerity, a thief of vows, a thief of appearance, and a thief of conduct and disposition, who performs the "debauchery of the gods" (devakibbisa). (Dasavē. 220–221)
Even after attaining the state of a god, he is reborn among the *devakibbisa* gods;
even there, he does not know: "What deed of mine has brought this fruit?
Then, having fallen from that state as well, he will obtain the condition of an *elamūyaga*.
"In hell or in the animal realm, where enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain" (Dasavē.
223). Having seen this fault, the Wise One, the Son of the Nāgas, declared: "One should avoid even a slight measure of deceitful falsehood" (Dasavē. 224).
Having learned the purification of the search for alms from the presence of the self-restrained Buddhas, there a monk, with well-directed mind, intense shame, and possessed of virtues, should dwell.
Thus I say. (Dasavēyāliya 225)
[The Great Story of the Hero] Endowed with knowledge and vision, he exerted himself in self-restraint and austerity.

To him who was perfected in the calculation of the scriptures and had arrived at the park, kings and royal ministers, brahmins, or even kshatriyas, being tranquil in soul, asked: "How is your sphere of conduct? (Dasavē. 226–227)
For them, he—tranquil, self-controlled, bringing happiness to all beings, well-disciplined in the training, and discerning—declares:
"Listen to me regarding the Nigganthas who seek the Dharma, wealth, and pleasure. (Dasavē. 228)
The entire range of conduct is formidable and difficult to master;

nothing else has been declared [by the Jinas] that is so extremely difficult to practice as this, which belongs to one who possesses vast standing—[a state] that has not existed before and will not exist again. (Dasavē. 229–230)

Listen to how those qualities which must be maintained unbroken and unimpaired by monks—whether they be young or mature, or even those who are ill—are to be practiced. (Dasavē. 231) There are eighteen points which a fool violates.
In that regard, one falls away from the state of a *nirgrantha* due to one of these [causes]. (Dasavē.
232) Among these, this is the first cause, taught by the Great Hero:
non-violence is seen as subtle; it is restraint toward all living beings. (Dasavē. 233)
As many living beings as there are in the world, whether mobile or stationary,
one should not kill them nor cause them to be killed, whether knowingly or unknowingly. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 234) All living beings desire to live, not to die.
Therefore, the Nigganthas avoid that terrible taking of life. (Dasavē.

235) Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another, whether out of anger or even out of fear, one should not speak a lie to harm others, nor should one cause another to speak it. (Dasavē. 236)
Falsehood in this world is censured by all virtuous men and causes a lack of trust among living beings; therefore, one should avoid lying. (Dasavē.
237) Whether it be animate or inanimate, whether small or great—

Even regarding something as small as a tooth-stick, those who have not received formal permission do not take it themselves, nor do they cause others to take it, nor do they approve of another taking it; such are the self-restrained ones. (Dasavē. 238–239)
The sages in this world do not practice terrible unchastity, which is a negligence poorly maintained; they avoid the source of fear and the cause of division.
This is the root of demerit, a heap of great faults. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 240)
Therefore, the Nirgranthas avoid association with sexual intercourse. (Dasavē.

241) They do not desire the storage of salt that is pressed or extracted, nor oil, ghee, or molasses; these are the followers of the Son of the Nāya clan who have cast off worldly attachments. (Dasavē. 242)

The pursuit of wealth is a secondary affliction; whatever else there may be that involves the proximity of sensual pleasures, one who indulges in these is neither a householder nor a renunciant. (Dasavē.
243) Even as for a robe, a bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth...

Even that which they maintain and carry out of restraint and modesty is not called "possession" by the Protector, the Son of the Nāya clan; rather, infatuation is said to be possession—thus it was stated by the Great Seer. (Dasavē. 244–245)
The Buddhas, who carry all things [with equanimity], do not practice the notion of "mine" even toward their own bodies, let alone toward protection or possession.
Aho! The practice of austerity has been praised by all the Buddhas as eternal.
That livelihood which is consistent with modesty, and eating but a single meal; (Dasavē.
247) There are subtle living beings for me, whether mobile or stationary, which one does not see at night; how then could one practice the search for food [at that time]? (Dasavē. 248)
"Moist with water, mixed with seeds, and with living beings fallen upon the ground—these a restrained one should avoid;
how could one wander there at night?
Having seen this fault, it was spoken by the Son of the Jñātis.
The Nirgranthas do not consume any food at night. (Dasavē.
250) The self-controlled ones, well-composed, do not harm the earth-element by means of mind, speech, or body, through the threefold application of action. (Dasavē. 251)

One who harms the earth-body also harms other similar beings and various types of mobile creatures, both those with eyes and those without eyes. Therefore, having understood this, [one should avoid] the fault that increases rebirth in evil states. (Dasavēyāliya 252)

One should avoid the undertaking of violence against the earth-body for as long as life lasts. (Dasavēyāliya 253) The self-controlled ones, well-composed, do not harm the water-body by means of mind, speech, or body, through the threefold application of action. (Dasavēyāliya 254)
By harming the water-element, one harms other beings of that same nature and various other mobile creatures, both those with eyes and those without eyes.
Therefore, having understood this, [one should avoid] the fault that increases rebirth in miserable states. (Dasavēyāliya 2.55)
One should avoid the undertaking of violence against the water-body for as long as life lasts. (Dasavē.
256) They do not desire fire, which blazes with a sharp weapon of one kind or another, which is difficult to approach from any side. (Dasavē. 257)

Whether to the east or to the west, upward or toward the intermediate directions, below or to the south, or even to the north—this fire is a destroyer of living beings; there is no doubt about it. (Dasavē.
Therefore, those who are established in right conduct and self-restraint should not undertake anything [involving fire].
Having understood this, one should avoid for as long as life lasts the undertaking of the fire-body, which is a fault that increases rebirth in miserable states. (Dasavē. 259–260)
The Buddhas consider the fanning of the wind to be such that it is full of fault; this is not to be practiced by the virtuous.
(Dasaveyāliya 261) Whether with a fan, a leaf, or a branch-fan, [one should not cause a breeze].
They do not wish to weave, nor do they have others weave for them. (Dasavē.
262) Even regarding a robe, a bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth, they do not cause these to be woven, and they avoid causing injury. (Dasavē. 263)

Therefore, having understood this, one should avoid for as long as life lasts the undertaking of violence against the air-body, which is a fault that increases rebirth in miserable states. Those who do not harm the vegetable kingdom by thought, word, or deed— *Dasavaikālika Sūtra* 2.64.

By means of the threefold application of activity, the self-restrained ones who are well-concentrated—when harming the vegetable kingdom, they harm other various living beings that are mobile, both those with eyes and those without eyes. (Dasavē. 265–266)
Therefore, having understood this, one should avoid for as long as life lasts the undertaking of forest-dwelling, which is a fault that increases rebirth in miserable states. (Dasavē.
267) They do not harm the body of mobile beings by mind, speech, or body.
Through the application of the threefold activity, the self-restrained ones are well-composed. By harming the body of mobile beings,
one harms those very beings and various other living creatures, both those with eyes and those without eyes.

Therefore, having understood this, one should avoid for as long as life lasts the undertaking of violence against the mobile-bodied beings, which is a fault that increases rebirth in miserable states. (Dasavē. 270) Regarding the four kinds of food that a sage may consume...
Avoiding these [faults], one should maintain self-restraint. (Dasavē.
271) Regarding alms-food, bedding, clothing, and fourthly, water itself—one should not desire what is not permissible; one should accept only what is permissible. (Dasavē. 272)
"Those who claim ownership over sacrifices, and who approve of what is bought, prepared for a specific person, or brought by force—so it was said by the Great Seer.
Therefore, [one should avoid] food and drink that is bought, prepared for a specific person, or brought by force. (Dasaveyāliya 273)
The self-controlled soul, a Nirgrantha living by the Dharma, avoids what is blameworthy. (Dasavē.
274) Furthermore, one who eats food and drink from bronze vessels, bronze bowls, or even from jars, falls away from right conduct. (Dasavē. 275)
In the undertaking of cold water for bathing and the discarding of water used for washing oneself, there are living beings that perish; thus, lack of restraint is seen therein.
Subsequent action and prior action—these may not be appropriate in that case. (Dasaveyāliya 276)

Nirgranthas do not consume such things from the vessels of householders. (Dasavē. 277) It is unbecoming for those who are modest to sit or lie down on high couches, on thrones, or on beds adorned with garlands. (Dasavē. 278)
The Nirgranthas, established in the teachings of the Buddha, do not sit on benches or thrones, nor on seats or stools, because they have not inspected them;
these [beings] are difficult to discern, for life is profound and hard to perceive. (Dasavē. 279)

Having avoided such things as high seats and luxurious couches, for one who has entered the alms-round, if a seat of this kind is permitted, he incurs a transgression of the conduct of an ascetic. (Dasaveyāliya 280–281)
The turning away from celibacy, the killing of living beings, the obstructing of mendicants, and the provocation of householders;
lack of restraint regarding celibacy, or even the suspicion concerning women. (Dasaveyāliya 282)

One should avoid from afar that place which increases idleness. (Dasavē. 283) For one who is overcome by old age, or for an ascetic who is afflicted by illness, the use of a seat is permitted for any one of the three [types of practitioners]. (Dasavē. 284)
Whether sick or healthy, he who desires a bath has overstepped his conduct;
his self-restraint is destroyed. (Dasaveyāliya 285) These living beings are subtle, dwelling in the dust and in the crevices.
If a monk, while bathing, should cause water to splash about;
therefore they do not bathe, for as long as life lasts we observe the formidable vow of non-bathing, whether with cold or warm water. (Dasavē. 286–287)
They never at any time practice bathing, nor the use of unguents, nor rubbing with oil, nor the application of lotus-powders for the sake of cleansing the body.
Even though they are naked, shaven-headed, and have long hair and nails... (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 288)
For one who has desisted from sexual intercourse, what purpose is served by adornment? (Dasavē.
289) A monk who engages in the activity of adornment binds thick karma in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, by which he falls into that which is difficult to cross. (Dasavē. 290)

The Buddhas consider such [conduct] to be directed toward ornamentation; it is full of blame and is not practiced by the self-controlled. Those who see the self as delusion, devoted to austerity, practice the virtues of restraint and uprightness. (Dasaveyāliya 291)
They shake off the evils committed in the past, and they do not commit new evils. (Dasavē.

292) Tranquil, free from possessiveness, and owning nothing, possessing true knowledge along with its realization, and renowned for their glory—like the moon risen clear and stainless—they, the protectors, attain perfection and celestial mansions. (Dasavē. 293)
Thus I say.
[Purity of Speech]
Having thoroughly examined the four types of speech, the wise person should train in the discipline of two; however, two [types of speech] should not be uttered at all. (Dasavē.
294) That which is true but unfit to be spoken, and that which is mixed truth and falsehood—[these should not be spoken].
A wise person should not speak that which has not been practiced by the Buddhas. (Dasavē.
295) A wise person should speak speech that is neither false nor untrue, which is truthful, blameless, and not harsh; speech that is well-considered and free from doubt. (Dasavē. 296)
Whether it be this eighth [type of speech] or any other that is called eternal—whether it be true or false—the wise man should avoid even that. (Dasavē.
297) Whatever speech a man utters that is contrary to fact, yet appears to be as it is...
Therefore, he is touched by evil; how much more so for one who speaks falsehood? (Dasavē.
298) "Therefore we shall go," "we shall speak," "such-and-such will happen to us," "I shall do this," or "he shall do this"—(Dasavē. 299)
Whatever speech is of this nature, which is doubted regarding the past or the present matter, that too the wise man should avoid. (Dasavē.
300) Regarding the past time, the present, and the future...
But if one does not know what has been said, one should not say, "It is thus. (Dasavē.
301) And regarding the past time, the present, or the future—whatever matter there may be that causes doubt—one should not say of that, "It is thus. (Dasavē. 302)
Whatever has occurred in the past, and whatever may occur in the present or the future without doubt—this one should point out as being exactly thus.
Likewise, speech that is harsh and which causes heavy harm to living beings... (Dasavē. 303)
Even that [truth] should not be spoken, for it is the source of evil.

Likewise, one should not say of a one-eyed person, "You are one-eyed," nor of a eunuch, "You are a eunuch," nor of one suffering from disease, "You are sick," nor of a thief, "You are a thief. (Dasavēyāliya 304–305)
For this reason and for no other, a wise person who understands the faults of conduct and disposition should not speak that by which another is harmed:
"O plowman! or "O cowherd!", or "O dog! or "O Vasula! (Dasaveyāliya 306).
Whether it be in a state of distress or even in prosperity, a wise person should not speak thus:
"O Mother," "O Daughter-in-law," "O Mother's Sister," "O Father's Sister," "O Brother's Daughter," "O Daughter," or "O Granddaughter. (Daśavaikālika 307–308)
One should not address a woman as "Hale," "Halletti," "Annotti," "Bhatte," "Sāmini," "Gomini," "Hole," "Gole," or "Vasule.
Rather, one should address her by her given name or, alternatively, by her family name. (Dasaveyāliya 309)
Having ascertained what is appropriate, one should speak or converse [with others].
One should address them as "Venerable Sir" (ajja) or "Worthy Sir" (pajja), or as "Father," "Little Father," "Maternal Uncle," "Nephew," "Son," or "Daughter-in-law. (Dasavēyāliya 310–311)
O sir! O ploughman! O sower! O master! O lord!
O cowherd! O hola! O gola! O vasula!—one should not address a man with such [terms].
Rather, one should call him by his name, or else by his family name (*purisagotta*). (Dasavē. 312)
Having approached appropriately, one should speak or converse [only after ascertaining the gender]. (Dasavē.

313) Regarding five-sensed living beings, one should say "this is a female" or "this is a male" only when one knows it; as long as one does not know it, one should say "it is a living being. (Dasavē. 314)
Likewise, regarding a human, an animal, a bird, or even a reptile that is large, fat, or destined for slaughter—one should not say, "It is fat.
One should say, "It is grown," or one should say, "It is increased. (Dasavē. 315)
Whether it be a female elephant or a bull, one should address it as "of great body.
Likewise, a wise person should not speak of a cow as "difficult to milk," "to be tamed," "a milch-cow," "a beast of burden," or "fit for a chariot. (Dasaveyāliya 316–317)

One should say, "A young cow," or "A milch cow," or "A secret [cow]," or "A large one," or "A carrier" when referring to a cow. Likewise, one should go to gardens, mountains, and forests. (Dasavē. 318)
Seeing large trees, a wise person should not speak thus:
"Enough with pillars made of stone, archways, houses, door-bolts, and shutters; enough with water-tubs. (Dasavē. 319–320)
A stool, a water-pot, a plough, or something made of clay;
a staff for a traveler, or a navel-ring, or a block—these may suffice. (Dasavē.
321) One should know that a seat, a bed, a vehicle, or whatever else might be used as shelter.
A wise person should not speak speech that causes harm to living beings.
Likewise, when going to a garden, mountains, or forests, and seeing large trees, a wise person should speak thus: [Dasavēyāliya 322–323]
"These trees are long-lived, tall, massive, with spreading branches and thickets; they are beautiful to behold. Likewise, one should not eat fruits that are ripe or fit to be eaten raw. (Dasavē. 324)
One should not say of ripe fruits, "These are hanging from the trees.
One should say, "These mangoes are abundant," or "The fruits are very plentiful," or "They have grown in great quantity," or again, "They are like the forms of spirits. (Dasaveyāliya 325–326)
Likewise, one should not say of medicinal herbs: "They are ripe," "they have been harvested," "they are fit for the skin," "they are roasted," or "they are a snack of pihu. (Dasavē.
327) [One may say: "They have grown," "they have flourished abundantly," "they are firm," or "they are abundant."
One should address pregnant women as "those who have given birth," and [pregnant] cows as "those who have calved. (Dasavē.
328) Likewise, knowing that a feast is being prepared, one should not say, "Something must be done," nor should one say of a thief, "He is a robber," or of a river, "It has good fords. (Dasavē. 329)

One should not speak of "the festival" (saṅkhaḍi) as "the festival," nor call a thief "one who has attained his goal. One should explain that the bathing places of rivers are mostly crowded; likewise, one should not say of rivers that are full of water, "cross over. (Dasavē. 330)

One should not say, "I will cross by boat," nor should one say, "It is to be drunk with the hand. (Dasavēyāliya 331) A wise person should speak thus: "The river has many currents, it is difficult to plunge into, its waters overflow, and its waters are very vast. (Dasavēyāliya 332)

In the same way, having recognized that a blameworthy activity for another’s sake has not yet been completed, whether it is being done or already finished, the sage does not praise what is blameworthy. [He does not say:
"Well done!", "Well cooked!", "Well cut!", "Well fought!", or "Well killed! (Dasavē. 333).
"Having heard [the instruction], 'It is well-done,' the sage should avoid what is blameworthy. (Dasavē.

334) "As one who has carefully cooked [should not eat] what is half-cooked, as one who has carefully cut [should not use] what is half-cut, as one who has carefully polished [should not use] what is half-polished, so too, as one who has carefully struck [should not inflict] a deep wound, he should not inflict a deep wound upon the causes of karma. (Dasavē. 335)
Whether it be the most excellent or the most precious, there is nothing such as this that is unutterable or indescribable;
one should certainly not speak of what is unpraiseworthy. (Dasavē.
336) One should say, "I will tell all of this," but one should not say, "All of this."
Having investigated everything in every respect, a wise person should speak in this manner:

"It has been bought well" or "it has been sold well," "it is unsaleable" or "it is indeed saleable," "take this" or "let go of this"—he should not disclose the details of trade. (Daśavaikālika 337–338)

Whether of little value or great value, whether in buying or selling, when a commercial matter arises, one should explain it without fault. Likewise, a wise person, remaining unattached, may say, "Come," or "Do this. (Dasavē. 339)
"I shall stand; you go"—a wise person should not speak thus. (Dasavē.
340) "Many here are non-ascetics, yet they are called 'ascetics' in the world. One should not say that a non-ascetic is an ascetic; one should address an ascetic as an "ascetic. (Dasavē. 341)
One endowed with knowledge and vision, possessed of self-restraint and austerity,
and thus equipped with such virtues— one who is self-controlled, him one should honor. (Dasaveyāliya 3.42) Amidst the conflicts of gods, humans, and animals...
One should not say, "May there be victory for these," or "May it not be so. (Dasavē.
343) One should not say that wind or rain, cold or heat, safety or harm, or peace will "certainly be" or "will not be. (Dasavē. 344)
In that same way, O man, one should not utter the words "god of gods" regarding a cloud or a phenomenon in the sky;
whether it has ceased, risen, or is proceeding, one should say "the rain-cloud has rained," or simply "the atmosphere," or "that which moves through the secret [spaces]. (Dasavē. 345)
Seeing a person possessed of psychic power, one should address them as "possessed of psychic power. (Dasavē.
346) Likewise, one should not speak words that are censurable, provocative, discourteous, or harmful to others.
Out of anger, greed, fear, or laughter, or out of pride, one should not utter even a single word while laughing. (Dasavē. 347)

The sage, having attained purity of speech, should always avoid corrupt words; he should speak measuredly after due reflection on the meaning, and thus he receives praise in the midst of the wise. Having understood the faults and virtues of speech, one should always avoid that which is corrupt. (Dasavē. 348)
One should always strive for self-restraint in the six areas of conduct; one should speak words that are beneficial and conformable to the teachings of the Buddhas. (Dasavē.

349) Speaking with circumspection, with well-composed senses, having abandoned the four passions and being independent, he shakes off the dust and impurity accumulated in the past; thus he attains success in this world as well as the next. (Dasavē. 350)
Thus I say.
[The Discipline of Conduct]
Having attained the restraint of conduct, I shall explain to you, O monks, how it is to be practiced by a mendicant; listen to me in due order. (Dasavē.
351) Earth, water, fire, air, grass, trees, and seeds—
"Mobile beings are living creatures," so it was said by the Great Seer.
By maintaining a yoga of non-harming toward them, one should always be free from increase and decrease through mind, deed, and speech; thus does one become a restrained ascetic. (Dasavē. 352–353)
A self-controlled and well-composed monk should neither break nor scrape the earth, a wall, a stone, or a clod of earth by means of the three types of activity;
he should not sit on pure ground or on a seat covered with dust. (Dasavēyāliya 354)
Having wiped [the vessel] and having obtained permission from whomsoever it may be, he should sit down. (Dasavē.
355) He should not consume cold water, nor water fallen as rain upon stone, nor frost.
A self-controlled monk should accept only warm water that has been purified by heat. (Dasavē. 356)
If his own body becomes wet, the sage should neither wipe it nor rub it; he should simply endure it as it is, and not strike against it.
[He should avoid] glowing coals, fire, flames, or a firebrand that is still burning.
A sage should not fan himself, nor should he strike [the fire], nor should he extinguish it. (Dasavē.
358) With a palm-leaf fan, a leaf, a branch, or a whisk, one should not fan one's own body, nor any external substance. (Dasavē. 359)
One should not cut grass or trees, nor the fruit or root of anything; one should not even mentally long for various kinds of unripe seeds.
One should not stand in thickets, nor among seeds or green plants.
One should never harm living beings, whether in water or in dew-drops and mold; neither by speech nor by action should one injure moving creatures.
Remaining detached toward all beings, one should observe the manifold world. (Dasavē. 361–362)
There are eight subtle things to be observed, which a restrained monk who is intent on compassion for living beings should know, whether walking, standing, or sitting.
What are these eight subtle things? Those which a restrained monk should inquire about.
A wise and discerning person should explain these eight subtle things:
moisture, the subtle flower, minute living beings, mold, seeds, green plants, and the eighth is the subtle egg. (Dasavē. 364–365)
Thus one should know these things; being restrained in every way, vigilant, and always striving, with all senses composed. (Dasavē.
366) One should regularly inspect the foot-cloth with care.
The place for study and the ground for excrement, as well as the bedding or the seat—[these should be inspected].
Having inspected what is suitable regarding excrement, urine, spittle, mucus, and sweat, the self-restrained one should dispose of it. (Dasavē. 367–368)
Having entered another's house for the sake of food or drink, one should remain vigilant, speak with moderation, and not fix the mind upon forms.
One hears much with the ears and sees much with the eyes. (Dasavēyāliya 3.69)
A monk ought not to declare everything that has been seen or heard. (Dasavē.
370) Whether it be heard or seen, he should not speak what is harmful; nor should he, by any means, practice what is associated with householders. (Dasavē. 371)
Whether asked or unasked, whether it concerns something auspicious or something evil, one should not point out gain or loss; nor,
being greedy for food, should one wander for alms while speaking.
One should not consume what is unwholesome—whether it be bought, specially prepared for oneself, or brought from elsewhere;
nor should one store up anything, even in the slightest degree. Being self-restrained, living by right speech, and unattached, one should depend upon the world [for sustenance]. (Dasavē. 373–374)

Having heard the teaching of the Jina, one should be of simple livelihood, well-contented, few in desires, and easy to support; one should not fall into a state of cruelty, nor should one allow affection to settle upon sounds that are pleasant to the ear. (Dasaveyāliya 3.75)
One should endure with the body harsh and cruel sensations.
One should endure hunger, thirst, an uncomfortable bed, cold, heat, discontent, and fear without being overwhelmed;
for bodily suffering bears great fruit. (Dasavē. 376–377)

When the sun has set on the mountain and has not yet risen in the east, one should not even mentally desire any food or other requisites. (Dasavē. 378) One should be free from craving, steady, speaking little, and moderate in eating.
One should have one's belly guarded and one's teeth [restrained]; having obtained only a little, one should not complain.
One should not despise others outwardly, nor should one exalt oneself;
upon gaining a good reputation, one should not be arrogant on account of birth, asceticism, or intelligence. (Dasavēyāliya 379–380)

Whether knowingly or unknowingly, having committed an unrighteous act, one should quickly restrain oneself and not practice that second time. Having committed an improper act, one should neither conceal it nor deny it. (Dasaveyāliya 3.8–9)
Always being straightforward in disposition, unattached, and with senses subdued, one should speak words free from delusion to the noble-souled teacher;
having grasped that [instruction] through speech, one should put it into practice through action. (Daśavaikālika 382–383)
Having understood that life is unstable and having discerned the path to perfection, one should turn away from enjoyments, for one’s own lifespan is limited;
likewise, one should consider one’s own strength, vigor, fame, and health. (Dasaveyāliya 3.8–9)
Having understood the [proper] place and time, one should thus apply oneself. (Dasavē.
385) As long as old age does not afflict, as long as disease does not increase, and as long as the sense faculties do not decline, so long should one practice the Dharma. (Dasavē. 386)

One who desires their own welfare should vomit out these four visible things: anger, pride, deceit, and greed, which increases evil. (Dasavēyāliya 387) Anger destroys friendship; pride is the destroyer of humility.

Deceit destroys friends; greed is the destroyer of everything. (Dasaveyāliya 388) One should conquer anger through tranquility, pride through gentleness, deceit through uprightness, and greed through contentment. (Dasaveyāliya 389)
Anger and pride, when unrestrained, and deceit and greed, when increasing—
these four intense passions water the roots of rebirth.
One should practice humility toward those who are royal, and one should never abandon constant steadfastness in virtue.
Like a tortoise, guarding his limbs by drawing them close together, he should exert himself in austerity and self-restraint.
(Dasavēyāliya 391) He should not value sleep highly; he should avoid laughter and take no pleasure in mutual conversation.
He should always delight in the study of the scriptures. (Dasavēyāliya 392)

One who is diligent and constantly engaged in the practice of the ascetic’s duty attains the unsurpassed goal; that which is beneficial for both this world and the next, by which one goes to a happy state. (Dasaveyāliya 393)
One should attend upon the learned and inquire about the determination of the meaning.
Having restrained the hands, feet, and body, with senses subdued and guarded in his posture, the sage should sit in the presence of the teacher. (Dasavēyāliya 394–395)

One should not stand to the side of the teacher, nor in front, nor behind his tasks, nor touching his thigh; one should remain near the teacher. Without being asked, one should not speak, nor interrupt one who is speaking.
One should not eat meat from the back; one should avoid deceitful falsehood.
One should not speak anything that would cause offense, or by which another might quickly become angry; one should entirely avoid speech that leads to harm.

One who possesses self-control should utter speech that is seen, measured, and beyond doubt; complete, true, beneficial, and free from agitation. [Dasavē. 399] One who upholds the *Ācāra-prajñapti* and has studied the *Dṛṣṭivāda*.
Having perceived a lapse in solitude, the sage should not mock it. (Dasavē.
400) He should not explain to householders the stars, dreams, planetary conjunctions, omens, mantras, or medicines; such speech involves injury to living beings. (Dasavē. 401)

A dwelling that is well-provided with food, furnished with beds and seats, endowed with a place for excrement, and free from women and animals; [such a place] should be a secluded lodging, and one should not engage in conversation with women. (Dasavēyāliya 4.2)
One should not form intimacy with householders; one should form intimacy with the virtuous.
Just as a hen has constant fear of the hawk, so indeed does the practitioner of celibacy have fear of the female form. (Dasaveyāliya 403–404)
One should not gaze at the body of a woman, nor even at one well-adorned;
having seen her, one should withdraw the gaze as if seeing a blazing coal.
