(Dasavēyāliya 405) [One should avoid] a woman whose hands and feet have been cut off, or whose ears and nose have been mutilated.

A practitioner of celibacy should avoid even a naked woman. (Dasaveyāliya 406) For a man seeking his own welfare, adornment, association with women, and rich, flavorful food are like a deadly poison on a palm-leaf. (Dasaveyāliya 407)

One should not gaze upon the configuration of the limbs and members of women—their beautiful speech and glances—which increases sensual passion. One should not allow affection to settle upon pleasant sense objects. (Dasaveyāliya 4.8)
Having understood their impermanence and the transformation of persons;
having known the transformation of persons exactly as it is, one should dwell with craving subdued, having become cooled within oneself. (Dasavēyāliya 409–410)

Having gone forth with faith into that supreme state of the religious life, one should maintain those very qualities approved by the Teacher. One should always uphold this austerity, the practice of self-restraint, and the application to sacred study. (Dasavēyāliya 4.11)

Just as one who is skilled in weaponry and fully equipped with arms is sufficient for himself and sufficient for others, so it is for the protector who delights in study and meditation, who is free from evil states, and who is devoted to austerity;
whatever impurity he previously committed is purified by him, just as the dross of silver is blown away by fire. (Dasaveyāliya 4.12–4.13)

He who is such a conqueror of the senses, enduring suffering, endowed with wisdom, free from the sense of "mine," and possessing nothing—shines forth when the cloud-mass of karma has vanished, like the moon when the entire veil of clouds has disappeared. Thus I say. (Dasavē. 414)
[The loss of discipline through concentration:
Due to pride, anger, deceit, or negligence, one does not learn discipline in the presence of the teacher.
That very same state of being a non-human (an *abhūta*) becomes his own destruction, like the fruit of the *kīya* tree.
Those who, perceiving the teacher as "stupid," or knowing them to be "young" and "of little learning," treat them with contempt while embracing falsehood, commit an offense against their teachers.

Some may be dull by nature, yet even those who are young may be endowed with learning and intelligence, possessed of proper conduct, and whose souls are well-established in virtue; such persons, when insulted, may respond with fiery words.
Furthermore, he who, perceiving a Naga to be "young," treats him with contempt, brings about his own harm. (Dasaveyāliya 4.17)
Indeed, by disparaging even such a teacher, the dull-witted one surely enters the path of rebirth. (Dasavē.
418) Or even a highly enraged venomous serpent—what greater harm could it do than the destruction of life?
But when the feet of the teacher are displeased, there is no hope for enlightenment; there is no liberation. (Dasavē. 419)
One might step into a blazing fire, or one might provoke a venomous serpent;
or one who seeks to live might consume poison—yet such things are not equal to the offense of insulting one's teachers.
For even if one were to enter that fire, it might not burn him; and even if the venomous serpent were enraged, it might not devour him. (Dasaveyāliya Sutta 4.20)
Hālāhala poison might not kill, nor might one die from the severe reproach of a teacher. (Dasavē.
421) He who wishes to split a mountain with his head, or would awaken a sleeping lion, or would strike a blow at the tip of a spear—this is the analogy for insulting one's teachers. (Dasavē. 422)
One might indeed split even a mountain with one's head; a lion, when enraged, might not kill;
one might not pierce the tip of a spear; yet there is no liberation for one who insults his teacher. (Dasavē.
423) Furthermore, if the feet of the teacher are displeased, there is no liberation through disrespect.
Therefore, one who desires the happiness of freedom from affliction should take delight in being oriented toward the grace of the Guru.

(Dasaveyāliya 424) Just as one whose fire has been kindled pays homage to the flame when it is sprinkled with the clarified butter of various oblations, so too should one attend upon the Teacher, even though one has already attained infinite knowledge. (Dasaveyāliya 425)

One who studies the verses of the Dharma with reverence should also apply himself to the conduct of a venerable one; he should honor him with his head bowed and palms joined, constantly with body, speech, and mind. (Dasavē.
426) Modesty, compassion, self-restraint, and celibacy are the bases of purification for one who possesses merit.
Those teachers who constantly instruct me, them I honor constantly. (Dasavē.

427) Just as the sun, garlanded with heat, illuminates the entire world when it has set [in the sky], even so does the teacher shine through his learning, virtue, and wisdom, like Indra in the midst of the gods. (Dasavē. 428)

Just as the moon, joined with the autumn season and surrounded by a multitude of constellations and stars, shines in a cloudless, stainless sky, so does the leader of the group shine in the midst of the monks. (Dasavē.
429) The great sage, the teacher, is established in the yoga of meditative concentration through his learning, virtue, and wisdom.
Desiring to attain the unsurpassed [states], the seeker of Dharma should please and satisfy [the teacher].
Having heard well-spoken words, the wise one, being heedful, should serve the teacher;
having cultivated numerous virtues, he attains the unsurpassed perfection. (Daśavaikālika 4.30–31)
Thus I say:

From the root arises the trunk of the tree; from the trunk, afterwards, the branches grow; from the branches, the twigs and leaves; and from those, the flower, the fruit, and the sap. (Dasavēyāliya 4.32)
Thus, discipline is the root of the Dharma; it is its supreme liberation, by which one quickly attains fame, learning, and everything in its entirety. (Dasavē.
433) But he who is fierce, violent, stubborn, harsh in speech, deceitful, and fraudulent...
That person of undisciplined self is drowned, just as one who has entered a torrent of water. (Dasavē.
434) Even if he is disciplined, if a man becomes angry when urged by some means, he will lose his divine glory; [the teacher] should restrain him with punishment. (Dasavē. 435)

In the same way, those of undisciplined self who are reborn as horses or elephants are seen suffering while subjected to the yoke. Likewise, those of well-disciplined self who are reborn as horses or elephants [are not so afflicted].
In this world, men and women who have disciplined themselves are seen enduring happiness, having attained prosperity and great renown. (Dasavē.
437) Likewise, those of undisciplined self—men and women—are seen enduring suffering in this world, their radiance faded and their senses impaired. (Dasavē. 438)

Wasted by sticks and weapons, distressed by harsh words, their desires ruined, and overcome by hunger and thirst— just so are men and women in this world who have well-disciplined themselves. (Dasavēyāliya 4.39)
Those who have subdued their senses are seen attaining prosperity and great renown;
likewise, those of undisciplined self—gods, yakṣas, and guhyakas—are seen suffering when they are subjected to the power of others' will. (Dasaveyāliya 440–441)
In the same way, those who have well-disciplined themselves are seen by the gods, yakṣas, and guhyakas as they pass away peacefully, having attained prosperity and great renown. (Dasavē.
442) Those who are obedient to their preceptors and teachers and act according to their words...
Their training flourishes like trees watered with liquid. (Dasavē.
443) Crafts for one's own sake or for the sake of others, as well as technical skills, are for the enjoyment of householders and for the sake of this world. (Dasavē. 444)
Those who, while training, undergo bondage, terrible danger, and harsh suffering, are disciplined and have their senses well-restrained;
they honor that teacher for the sake of that craft. (Dasavē. 445)
They honor him with respect, being satisfied as those who carry out his instructions. (Dasavē.
446) How much more so for one who is a retainer of what has been heard and desires infinite welfare?
Whatever the teacher says to the monk, therefore he should not disregard it. (Dasavē. 447)
One should go to the bed, the path, the standing place, and the seats; one should bow at the feet and offer a salutation with joined palms.
(Dasavēyāliya 4.48) Having touched [the monk] with the body, as well as with the robes...
"Forgive my offense, and I shall not speak thus again. (Dasavē.
449) Or as a draft animal, driven by the goad, pulls the chariot;
so too does one of evil intellect do what he is told when repeatedly urged. (Dasavē. 450)

Whether they speak or chatter, the wise man should not respond while seated; having risen from his seat, he should respond with a desire to listen. Having examined the proper time, the intention, the conduct, and the reasons [for speaking], [he should respond]. (Dasavēyāliya 4.51)
By whatever means possible, one should strive for that [discipline]. (Dasavē.
452) The downfall of the undisciplined and the attainment of the disciplined— he who understands this duality attains the training. (Dasavē. 453)

Furthermore, for one who is fierce, arrogant with pride, malicious, a man who disregards commands, who has not seen the Dharma, is unskilled in discipline, and does not share [his gains], there is truly no liberation.
But he who follows the instructions of his teachers, who has mastered the Dharma through study, and is skilled in discipline—[for him there is liberation]. (Dasaveyāliya 4.54)
Having crossed over this flood so difficult to cross, and having exhausted their karma, they have gone to the supreme state. Thus I say. (Dasavē.
455) One who desires to learn should attend upon the teacher as one attends a blazing fire, remaining ever vigilant.
He who, having observed and understood even a mere gesture, fulfills the teacher's wish, is worthy of honor. (Dasavē.

456) One who applies discipline for the sake of self-purification, listening attentively while grasping the words, desiring [the goal] exactly as it has been taught, and not deceiving the teacher—he is worthy of honor. (Dasavē. 457)

He who offers humility toward those of long standing, and who behaves with deference toward even those junior in seniority, who is truthful in speech, respectful, and modest—he is worthy of honor. (Dasavē.
458) He wanders for pure alms unknown to others, and always collects his food solely for the purpose of sustaining life.

One who does not lament for what has not been obtained, and does not boast when something has been obtained, is worthy of honor. (Dasavēyāliya 459) He who, even when there is a lack of bedding, lodging, seats, food, and drink, restrains himself through fewness of desires despite this non-attainment, and remains devoted to contentment as his primary practice—he is worthy of honor. (Dasavēyāliya 460)

Thorns made of iron can be endured by a man with hope and effort; but he who endures thorns made of speech—arrows piercing the ear—is truly worthy of honor. (Dasaveyāliya 4.61) Indeed, iron thorns cause only momentary pain, and they are easily extracted from there.

Words that are difficult to utter and even more difficult to withdraw cause a succession of enmities and lead to great fear. Those who, though restrained in their speech, cause distress when their words reach the ear, are not worthy of praise. But he who, being a supreme hero in the highest Dharma and having conquered his senses, endures such things—he is truly venerable. (Dasaveyāliya 4.62–4.63)
One who never speaks disparagingly of another behind their back, nor speaks face-to-face with hostility, nor utters speech that is degrading, unpleasant, or harmful, is always worthy of honor.
One who is not greedy, not deceitful, not dishonest, not slanderous, and whose livelihood is free from harm is likewise worthy.
One who is neither a worldly being nor one whose soul is cultivated [by worldly things], and who is always free from curiosity—that person is worthy of honor. (Dasavē.
465) A true ascetic (*sādhu*) is defined by virtues, while one lacking them is not a true ascetic. Take up the virtues of a true ascetic and abandon those who are not;
having known oneself through the self, he who is equal toward passion and hatred is worthy of honor. (Dasavē. 466)
In the same way, one should neither revile nor disparage anyone—whether young or old, a woman or a man, a monk or a householder; he who abandons pride and anger is worthy of honor. (Dasavē.
467) Those who are themselves honored always honor others, establishing them with effort as if settling an ear of grain.
Those ascetics who are worthy of honor, who have conquered their senses, and who are devoted to truth—they are venerable. (Dasavē.

468) Having heard the well-spoken words of those teachers, who are oceans of virtue, the wise sage should practice self-restraint, observing the five vows, being guarded in the three ways, and having transcended the four passions; he is venerable. (Dasavē. 469)

Having constantly served the Guru here, the sage—skilled in the subtle teachings of the Jina and proficient in understanding—shakes off the dust and impurity accumulated in the past and attains the radiant, supreme state. Thus I say. (Dasavēyāliya 4.70)

I have heard, O venerable one, that it was thus declared by the Blessed One: "In this world, indeed, four bases of discipline and composure (*vinaya-samādhi-sthāna*) have been proclaimed by the venerable Elders. What, then, are those four bases of discipline and composure proclaimed by the venerable Elders? These, indeed, are the four bases of discipline and composure proclaimed by the venerable Elders, namely: discipline and composure, learning and composure, austerity and composure, and conduct and composure.
In discipline, in learning, in austerity, and in conduct, the wise are ever steadfast."

Those who have conquered their senses delight their own souls. (Dasavēyāliya 472) Indeed, there are four kinds of discipline-concentration (*vinaya-samādhi*); namely: one listens attentively when being instructed; one correctly undertakes [the practice]; one fulfills the sacred word (*veda*); and one does not become self-conceited. This is the fourth point.
Regarding this, there is a verse:

He accepts the instruction of the heart and listens to it; furthermore, having mastered it, he does not become intoxicated by pride, remaining established in the tranquility of discipline. (Dasavē. 475) Indeed, the concentration of learning (*śruta-samādhi*) is fourfold, as follows: one should study with the thought, "Learning shall be mine"; one should study with the thought, "I shall become one-pointed in mind"; one should study with the thought, "I shall establish myself [in learning]"; and the fourth point is: one should study with the thought, "Being established myself, I shall establish others."
And there is a verse on this point:

"One who possesses knowledge with a one-pointed mind, being himself established [in concentration], establishes others [therein]; having studied the scriptures, he delights in the composure of learning. (Daśavaikālika 4.78)

The concentration of austerity is indeed fourfold; namely: one should not practice austerity for the sake of this world; one should not practice austerity for the sake of the next world; one should not practice austerity for the sake of fame, praise, reputation, or glory; one should practice austerity solely for the sake of the destruction of karma—this is the fourth point.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Always remaining in various virtues and austerities, free from desire, and intent on the destruction of karma."
Through austerity, he shakes off past evil; one who is disciplined and composed in austerity [Dasavē.

481]. Indeed, there are four kinds of composure in conduct (*āyāra-samāhī*): namely—(1) one should not practice conduct for the sake of this world; (2) one should not practice conduct for the sake of the next world; (3) one should not practice conduct for the sake of fame, praise, reputation, or renown; (4) one should practice conduct for no other reason than the reasons given by the Arhats. This is the fourth point. [And here there is a verse:
One who delights in the words of the Jina, who is free from greed, and who is established in a perfectly pure and noble self-restraint.
Restrained by the concentration of conduct, he becomes self-controlled and firm in his inner disposition. (Dasavē.
482) Having attained the fourfold concentration, thoroughly purified and with a well-composed mind, he brings about for himself vast benefit, happiness, and security. (Dasavē. 483)
One is liberated from birth and death; one completely abandons this state of existence and becomes an eternal Siddha, or a god with little passion and great power. Thus I say. (Dasaveyāliya 4.84)
When departing for their alms-round, the monks should always remain with their minds concentrated on the words of the Buddha.
He who does not fall under the power of women, and who does not swallow back what has been vomited—he is a bhikkhu. (Dasavē.

485) He who neither digs the earth nor causes it to be dug; who neither drinks cold water nor causes it to be drunk; and who, like a well-sharpened weapon, neither kindles fire nor causes it to be kindled—he is a bhikkhu. (Dasavē. 486)

He should not fan himself nor cause others to fan; he should not cut green plants nor cause them to be cut; always avoiding seeds, he should not consume anything with life—such a one is a monk. (Dasavē.
487) [For] there occurs the killing of mobile and immobile beings that depend upon earth, grass, and wood.
Therefore, he who does not eat what is specially prepared for him, nor causes it to be cooked, nor causes it to be prepared—such a one is a monk. (Dasavē.

488) Having wept at the words of the Son of the Jinas, he should regard the six classes of living beings as equal to himself; he who observes the five great vows and the restraint of the five influxes—such a one is a monk. (Dasavē. 489)

He who always restrains the four passions, remains steadfast in the words of the Buddha, is free from pride, possesses a nature like refined gold, and completely avoids household attachments—he is a monk. (Dasavē.
490) One with right view is always undeluded; for there truly exists knowledge, austerity, and self-restraint.
He who shakes off past evil through austerity, being well-restrained in mind, speech, and body—he is a bhikkhu. (Dasavē.

491) Likewise, having obtained various kinds of food, drink, soft food, or hard food, whether from his own people or others, he who neither stores it nor causes it to be stored—he is a bhikkhu. (Dasavē. 492)
Likewise, having obtained food, drink, or various kinds of chewables and non-chewables, he should eat them after sharing with his fellow monks;

having eaten, he should be devoted to sacred study—such a one is a true monk. (Dasavē. 493) He should not engage in contentious talk, nor should he become angry, but remain tranquil with his senses subdued. (Dasavē. 494)
He who is constantly restrained through yoga, who is tranquil and does not cause harm—he is a monk. (Dasavē.

494) He who indeed endures the thorns of the village—insults, blows, and threats—as well as terrifying and frightening sounds and laughter; he who endures both pleasure and pain with equanimity—he is a monk. (Dasavē. 495)

Having undertaken the meditative posture in a cemetery, he is not terrified upon seeing various frightening and awe-inspiring things; always devoted to manifold virtues and austerity, he who does not long for his own body is a monk. (Dasavē.
496) Even when his body is constantly abandoned and cast off, whether it be beaten, struck, or torn apart...
A sage should be even as the earth, free from worldly attachment and devoid of curiosity; he is a monk. (Dasavē.
497) Having overcome the afflictions with his body, he should uplift himself from the path of rebirth;
knowing birth and death to be a great terror, he delights in austerity and is equanimous—he is a monk. (Dasavē. 498)
Restrained in hand, restrained in foot, restrained in speech, with senses restrained,
devoted to the inner self, and well-composed in soul— he who understands the meaning of the scriptures is a monk.
Not infatuated with possessions, free from greed, seeking alms without prior arrangement, and free from impurity, he is a monk.
He who abstains from buying and selling, and who has abandoned all attachments—he is a monk. (Dasavē.
500) The monk should not be greedy, nor should he crave flavors; he should wander for alms and not long for life.
He should renounce prosperity, honor, and praise; he whose soul is established in stability and who is free from desire—he is a monk. (Dasavē. 501)

One should not say of another, "This person is immoral," nor should one say that which would cause anger; knowing that merit and demerit are individual to each, one should not exalt oneself—he is a monk. (Dasavēyāliya 5.2) One should not be intoxicated by birth, nor by beauty, nor by gain, nor be intoxicated by learning.
Having avoided all worldly desires, he who delights in the meditation on the Dharma—he is a monk. (Dasavē.
503) The great sage proclaims the higher path; established in the Dharma, he establishes others as well.
Having gone forth, he should avoid the marks of the unvirtuous, and he should not indulge in laughter or deceit—he is a monk. (Dasavē. 504)

The monk, whose soul is ever established in what is eternally beneficial, having severed that impure and non-eternal dwelling in the body—the bond of birth and death—attains the state from which there is no returning. Thus I say. (Dasavē. 5.5)
[The Responses]

In this world, O friend! for a renunciant who has arisen from suffering, whose mind is overcome by weariness toward self-restraint (*saṃyama*), and who has fallen into dejection (*ohāṇu*)—yet who is not truly dejected—these eighteen points must be thoroughly reflected upon as being like the goad for a swift horse, the hook for an elephant, or the sail for a ship. They are as follows: 1. "O friend! in this evil age, life is difficult to lead; the sensual enjoyments of householders are trivial and fleeting, and men are mostly addicted to sleep. 2. "Furthermore, these sufferings of mine will not persist for long. 3. "The honor shown by low-born people and the receiving back of what has been vomited. 4. "Dwelling in a lower state of existence. 5. "O friend! the Dharma of householders is indeed difficult to attain while living in the midst of a householder's life. 6. "Anxiety leads to one's ruin; planning leads to one's ruin. 7. "Household life is full of dangers; the religious life (*pariyāya*) is free from danger. 8. "Household life is bondage; the religious life is liberation. 9. "Household life is blameworthy; the religious life is blameless. 10. "The sensual enjoyments of householders are common property to many; merit and demerit are individual. 11. "O friend! the life of humans is impermanent, as flickering as a drop of water on the tip of a blade of grass. 12. "Indeed, much sinful karma has been committed. 13. "O friend! there is no liberation without experiencing the consequences of sinful deeds previously performed—which were ill-conducted and difficult to undo—unless one endures them, or consumes them through austerity, or wears them away through penance. 14. This is the eighteenth point. [And here there is a verse:]
When an ignoble person abandons the Dharma for the sake of sensual enjoyment, that fool, being infatuated with it, does not understand his own welfare.
When he is cast down, like Indra fallen to the ground... (Dasavēyāliya 5.7)
Having fallen away from all righteous dharmas, he later suffers remorse. (Dasavē.
508) When one who was worthy of veneration becomes unworthy of veneration—like a deity fallen from its station—he later suffers remorse. (Dasavē. 509)
When one is wealthy, later one becomes poor, like a king fallen from his kingdom; he then suffers remorse.
When one is honored, later one becomes dishonored. (Dasaveyāliya 5.10)
Like a merchant cast into a small village, he later suffers remorse.
(Dasaveyāliya 5.11) When he becomes old, his youth having passed away, like a fish that has swallowed the hook, he later suffers remorse. (Dasaveyāliya 5.12)

When one is afflicted by the anxieties of a bad family, like an elephant bound in captivity, he later suffers remorse. Surrounded by wife and children, he remains steeped in the continuity of delusion. (Dasaveyāliya 5.13)
Just as an elephant stuck in the mud suffers later,

so too would I suffer later if today, though being a leader of the community (*gaṇin*), possessed a developed soul and was well-learned, I were to take delight in the religious life (*pariyāya*) and in the conduct taught by the Jina. (Dasaveyāliya 514–515)
The religious life of the great seers—those who are disciplined and those who are not—is like the worlds of the gods; yet for those who are undisciplined, it is similar to the great hells.
Knowing that the supreme happiness of the disciplined in their religious life is comparable to that of the immortals, [one should strive for it]. *Daśavaikālika Sūtra* 5.16.

Knowing that suffering is supreme and beyond compare, one who is wise in the religious life (*paryāya*) should therefore find delight in it. (Dasavē. 517) Those of bad character and lax conduct despise one who has fallen from the Dharma and is stripped of glory—like a sacrificial fire that has gone out and lost its heat—as they would a snake whose fangs have been pulled out but which still possesses terrible venom. (Dasavē. 518)

In this very world, there is loss of Dharma, infamy, ill-repute, and an evil name among the multitude for one who has fallen from Dharma by practicing unrighteousness and whose wealth has been dissipated; his destiny is downward. Having enjoyed pleasures with a mind full of passion, and having committed much such lack of self-restraint—*Dasaveyāliya Sutta* 5.19.6.
One goes to a rebirth that is free from affliction, yet suffering; and for such a person, enlightenment is not easily attained again and again. (Dasavē.

520) For this being who is a denizen of hell, brought to suffering and dwelling in defilement, even a *palyopama* or a *sāgaropama* [of time] might pass away; how much more so, then, this mental anguish of mine? (Dasavē. 521)
"This suffering shall not be long for me; for living beings, the thirst for enjoyments is impermanent.
This [suffering] shall not persist through this body of mine, nor shall it persist through the remainder of my life.
(Dasaveyāliya 5.22) He whose self is thus firmly resolved would rather abandon his body than indeed the teaching of the Dharma.
Such a one as that, the senses do not shake, just as the winds cannot shake the well-seen mountain.

Thus perceiving this, a wise man, having understood the various means for his own welfare, should abide by the word of the Jina, guarded by the threefold restraint through deed, speech, and mind. (Dasavē. 523–524)
Thus I say.
[The Practice of Solitude]
I shall now expound the Cūlikā, the scripture spoken by the Kevalins;
having heard it, the wisdom regarding the Dharma arises in those of great merit.
When many people have set out following the current, one who has gained the skill to go against the current [must act accordingly].
The self must be directed against the current by one who desires to become liberated. (Dasavē.
526) The world is pleasant when following the current; for those of right conduct, the influx [of karma] is against the current.
Following the current is saṃsāra; against the current is its crossing over. (Dasavē. 527)

Therefore, through exertion in right conduct (*ācāra-parākrama*), and by being abundant in restraint (*saṃvara*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the modes of conduct (*caryā*), virtues (*guṇa*), and observances (*niyama*) of the ascetics (*sādhūnām*) are to be observed. [Dasavē.
5.28] Dwelling in non-fixed locations (*anīyasa-vāsa*), wandering for alms (*samudāna-caryā*), the practice of unknown alms-gathering (*annāta-uñcha*), and solitude (*paṭirikka*).
Avoiding disputes and quarrels, the wandering lifestyle of the sages is praised. (Dasavē.

529) Avoiding pride and arrogance, and [accepting] food and drink that are brought from afar and seen [to be pure], a monk should wander according to the appropriate practice; the ascetic should strive for such association with those of his own kind. (Dasavē. 530)

One should not consume liquor or meat, one should be free from stinginess, constantly practice non-attachment, frequently perform the *kāyotsarga* (posture of renunciation), and be devoted to the yoga of sacred study (*svādhyāya*).
One should not claim [ownership] over beds, seats, couches, mats, or likewise food and drink.
One should not harbor a sense of ownership toward anyone at all—whether in a village, a family, a city, or a country. (Dasavē.
532) A householder should not perform services for him, nor should he offer salutations, prostrations, or worship.
He should dwell together with those who are undefiled; thus the sage’s conduct shall suffer no decline. (Dasavē. 533)
If one cannot find a skillful companion who is superior in virtue or equal in virtue, one should wander alone, avoiding evil deeds and remaining unattached to sensual pleasures.
A year is the maximum limit; one should not dwell in that same place for a second year.
A monk should conduct himself according to the path of the Sūtra, just as the meaning of the Sūtra commands. (Dasavē.

535) In the period between the first part and the last part of the night, he should examine himself by means of himself: "What has been done by me? What remains of my duty? What is possible that I do not practice? (Dasavē. 536)
"What does another see in me, and what do I see in myself? Or, what lapse am I not avoiding?"—one who does not correctly observe in this way should not harbor attachment toward the future. (Dasavē.
537) Wherever one perceives something ill-applied, whether by body, speech, or mind...
Right there the wise man should withdraw [the senses], just as a skilled horseman quickly pulls back the reins. (Dasavē.

538) For that steadfast and virtuous man who always possesses such self-control over his faculties and discipline, him they call in this world one who lives awakened; he lives by the life of restraint. (Dasavē. 539)

The self must indeed be constantly guarded with all the senses well-composed. The unguarded self enters the path of rebirth; the well-guarded self is liberated from all sufferings. Thus I say. (Dasavaikālika Sūtra 5.40)
The *Dasaveyāliya Mūlasutta* has been thoroughly edited and compiled by the sage Dīparatnasāgara. It is complete.
